# Menisci

Two crescents of fibrocartilage that sit between the femur and the tibia.

## Junior

Your knee has two rubbery C shaped pads inside it. They sit between the thigh
bone and the shin bone. Picture a washer under a bolt. The pads spread the
squeeze across a wider area, so the smooth cartilage underneath lasts longer.
They also help the knee feel steady when you turn.

Each pad is thicker at its outer edge and thin at the inner edge. That wedge
shape stops the rounded end of the thigh bone from sliding off the flat top of
the shin bone. The pads are not fixed in place. They shift a little as the knee
bends, which keeps the contact area large through the whole range of movement.

The outer rim has a blood supply. The inner part has almost none, which is why
a tear near the middle heals badly. A tear can happen when a knee twists while
the foot stays planted, and it can also happen slowly as the tissue wears. If
your knee locks, swells or hurts to stand on, tell a parent, a teacher or a
coach, and have it checked by a health professional.

### Key learning points

- The menisci are two C shaped pads of tough cartilage in the knee.
- They spread load across a wider surface.
- The outer rim has a blood supply and the inner part has very little.

## Patient

The menisci are two wedges of fibrocartilage in the knee joint. The medial
meniscus is the larger and more C shaped of the pair. The lateral meniscus is
smaller, more circular, and it moves further during bending.

They share load between the thigh bone and the shin bone, add stability and
help spread joint fluid across the surfaces. Losing meniscal tissue raises the
pressure on the cartilage underneath, which is why surgeons now preserve
meniscal tissue wherever the tear allows it.

Blood reaches the outer third, so tears there can heal. The middle third has a
partial supply. The inner third has none, and tears there rarely heal on their
own. That pattern explains a great deal about treatment. A tear in the outer
rim may be repaired with sutures and given time. A tear in the inner part is
usually trimmed back to a stable edge, or left alone if it causes no symptoms.

Age matters too. A tear in a young knee after a twisting injury behaves
differently from a tear found on a scan in a knee that already shows wear. The
second kind is common, and it is often not the source of the pain. A scan
finding is read alongside the history and the examination, never on its own.

### Key learning points

- The medial meniscus is larger and less mobile than the lateral meniscus.
- The menisci share load, add stability and spread joint fluid.
- Only the outer third has a reliable blood supply.
- Removing meniscal tissue raises contact pressure on the cartilage.

### Frequently asked questions

**Q.** Does every meniscal tear need an operation?
No. Many settle with time and rehabilitation. A knee that locks is treated
differently from a knee that aches.

**Q.** Will the tear heal on its own?
A tear in the outer rim may heal. A tear in the inner part usually will not,
because the blood supply is not there.

**Q.** Can I still walk on it?
Many people can. Pain, swelling and locking are the signs that need review by a
clinician.

**Q.** Does a tear on a scan explain my pain?
Not always. Tears are found on scans of knees that do not hurt. The examination
and the history carry as much weight as the image.

## Medical student

Each meniscus is a semilunar fibrocartilage, roughly triangular in cross
section, attached to the tibial plateau at an anterior and a posterior root.
Circumferential collagen bundles convert axial load into hoop stress, which the
roots resist in tension [2]. Radial tie fibres run across those bundles and
stop the tissue splitting along its length.

The medial meniscus is anchored to the deep medial collateral ligament and to
the capsule, so it moves less than the lateral meniscus and is injured more
often in the chronically deficient knee. The lateral meniscus is separated from
the capsule by the popliteal hiatus and translates considerably further during
flexion [1]. The posterior horn of the medial meniscus acts as a secondary
restraint to anterior tibial translation, which is why it takes load in a knee
with a torn cruciate.

Vascularity follows the perimeniscal capillary plexus. The classical red, red
white and white zones describe the outer third, the middle third and the inner
third [1]. Nutrition of the inner zone depends on diffusion from synovial
fluid, and healing capacity follows the same gradient.

Composition is mostly water, with type one collagen making up the bulk of the
dry weight. Proteoglycan content is low compared with articular cartilage,
which suits a tissue loaded mainly in tension rather than compression [2].
Cell populations differ by zone, and the outer zone behaves more like
fibroblastic tissue while the inner zone behaves more like cartilage.

### Key learning points

- Hoop stress depends on intact anterior and posterior roots.
- A root avulsion behaves mechanically like a total meniscectomy.
- Medial meniscal mobility is limited by its capsular and ligamentous
  attachments.
- Type one collagen dominates the dry weight and suits tensile loading.
